timeline.action: Brian Schwanz, USD 232's Chief of Operations, sends a memo to the school board describing JCPRD's before-and-after-school program as 'invaluable to our families' and asks the board to approve the rental contract on its consent agenda.
USD 232's Board of Education approves the JCPRD lease agreement for the 2025-26 school year, including Section 8(d) requiring JCPRD to follow all school board policies.

BreAnna Burks (kindergarten staff) emails the parent: school policy does not mix age groups at recess; kindergartners stay on the green turf; there are typically 3-4 adult supervisors. She routes JCPRD concerns to the principal and Leigh White.

Parent replies to Burks: based on those policies, what Liam described should not have been possible. He asks whether the policy is always followed and notes the same third graders are involved in both the recess and JCPRD incidents.

Parent follows up: Liam called the recess and JCPRD incidents 'pranks.' Parent distinguishes imagination from dishonesty, thanks Leigh White for helping investigate, and commits to working with Liam on consequences.
A 9-year-old physically attacks Liam (age 6) on the Mize Elementary playground during the JCPRD aftercare program. Five JCPRD staff are outside. None of them witness the assault.

Leigh White (JCPRD site coordinator) sends the first response: says safety is a 'top priority,' the situation was 'handled,' staff have extensive training, and writes 'I am sorry you feel [child] is being harmed' — framing a documented battery as a matter of parental perception.

Parent fires back: this isn't a 'feeling' — JCPRD's own staff confirmed the battery. Liam's pediatrician has filed a DCF report. Parent announces plans to file a police report and a formal complaint with JCCL because JCPRD offered no details and no safety plan.
Parent files a report with the Shawnee Police Department. Case number: #2601522.

Parent emails Liam's teachers: Liam will be absent for the week on pediatrician's orders for close monitoring. Parent shares that DCF and police reports have been filed and that Liam will not return to JCPRD OST.
JCPRD manager calls the parent by phone and offers a copy of the finalized incident report.
Amy Branson (JCPRD staff) emails the parent the JCPRD incident form along with a refund notice.

Parent sends a detailed written rebuttal of the JCPRD incident report, pointing out: the report is based on hearsay, the witness list includes people who didn't see what happened, 'no medical treatment necessary' contradicts the pediatrician's assessment, the report calls the attack 'accidental' when Liam describes an intentional elbow drop, and the children were questioned together in the same room.

Jennifer Anderson (JCPRD Children's Services Manager) responds: the report was written the day of the incident; KDHE and licensing were notified when the parent mentioned medical care. She offers to meet.
Parent declines a meeting with JCPRD unless they first correct the incident report to reflect accurate facts.
Principal Balthazor emails about car loop logistics for picking up and dropping off Liam.

Parent sends a detailed safety email to school staff: five JCPRD staff were outside and none witnessed the assault; the pediatrician warned of near-miss spinal injury requiring a Level 1 trauma center if inflammation progressed; JCPRD won't remove the older student; parent demands a district investigation and requests 504 protections.

Principal Balthazor responds: JCPRD is a 'separate entity' that leases space and is not managed by the district after hours. She offers a school-day safety plan and 504 guidance, but declines jurisdiction over the aftercare incident.
Parent asks directly: is the district refusing to investigate? He confirms his prior email was a formal written request for a 504 evaluation.
Principal Balthazor routes the parent to Alvie Cater (Deputy Chief of Staff) for the incident inquiry and Janine Winters (school counselor) for the 504 process.

Parent sends a formal grievance letter to Alvie Cater, citing: the battery on school property, USD 232's anti-bullying policy, Kansas statute K.S.A. 72-6114, the lease agreement's constructive-possession implications, and documented prior notice of problems.
Alvie Cater responds and proposes an in-person meeting for Monday, April 13 at 1:00 PM at the district office in De Soto.

Parent accepts the meeting and sets expectations. He explains that Liam can't distinguish between JCPRD and the school day, notes the incidents occurred 'exclusively during the aftercare program,' and highlights that five staff were present yet none witnessed the assault.

Parent emails all school staff: quotes Lease Section 8(d) requiring JCPRD to follow board policies, raises fire-code concerns about mixing kindergartners with older children, describes the physical vulnerability of a 6-year-old's 'size and limited motor skills,' and demands the district investigate.
School counselor Janine Winters calls the parent by phone. The content of this call is not transcribed in any emails.

Janine Winters sends a follow-up email: attaches a 504 fact sheet and a counseling permission slip, and writes 'as I understood during our conversation, this is not the avenue you would like to move forward with at this time' — memorializing the parent's alleged 504 withdrawal based on the phone call.

Alvie Cater sends his detailed position: JCPRD operates independently with its own staff and policies; uses the parent's 'exclusively aftercare' language to argue it falls under JCPRD jurisdiction; lists JCPRD's KDHE critical incident steps; and states the parent 'declined' JCPRD's meeting offer.

Parent replies immediately: quotes Lease Section 8(d) word-for-word, explains he declined the JCPRD meeting because they refused to fix the inaccurate report, and asks whether any other agreement supersedes the lease obligations.
Parent forwards the full Leigh White / JCPRD email chain to Alvie Cater to provide complete documentation of the JCPRD interactions.

Parent sends his final email to Jennifer Anderson (JCPRD): closes the administrative channel, demands they amend the inaccurate report, conduct a proper investigation, and implement structural safety fixes. He attaches the full lease PDF.

Alvie Cater cancels the Monday meeting — the morning after the parent cited the lease. He writes: 'It sounds like we are not aligned on this.' He redirects the parent to JCPRD and KDHE, effectively shutting down the district's administrative resolution process.
Parent responds to Janine Winters: no one-on-one counselor sessions with Liam without a parent present; the family will use private providers. He discloses a pending lawsuit seeking equitable relief.

Dear Mr. Crowley,

Thank you for your email and for sharing detailed information about Liam’s
experience. I want to begin by acknowledging how concerning and upsetting
this situation must be for you and your family. The seriousness of what
you’ve described, as well as the potential for more severe injury, is not
lost on us. Liam’s safety and sense of security at school are extremely
important, and we take your concerns seriously.

I also want to clarify an important distinction regarding the before and
after-school program. Johnson County Parks and Recreation District (JCPRD)
operates this program as a separate entity that leases space within our
school. While the program takes place on school property, it is not managed
or supervised by the school district, and all staffing, policies, and
incident responses during that time fall under JCPRD’s authority. For
questions, concerns, or requests for action related to that program, we
recommend contacting Jennifer Anderson, Children’s Services Manager for
JCPRD, at 913-826-3015.

That said, we absolutely understand your concern about ensuring Liam’s
safety during the school day. We are committed to working with you
proactively to support Liam while he is under the school’s supervision.

We would be glad to partner with you to develop a comprehensive safety
plan that addresses Liam’s needs during the school day and at all
school-sponsored activities. This plan can include structured supervision
strategies, clear communication protocols, and reasonable measures to
minimize interactions as appropriate within the school setting.
Additionally, if you are interested in pursuing a 504 evaluation, we can
guide you through that process and ensure that any supports are
thoughtfully considered based on Liam’s health needs.

Our goal is to ensure that Liam feels safe, supported, and able to fully
participate in his school day. We welcome the opportunity to meet with you
to discuss next steps and begin developing a plan together.

Please let me know if you would like to schedule a time to meet, or feel
free to contact the school office so we can coordinate. Wishing you a
wonderful day!

Sincerely,



*Gerri Balthazor*

Principal

Mize Elementary

Thank you for the logistics regarding the car loop.

Our primary focus right now is Liam’s safety. JCPRD’s own report admits
that even though five staff members were supposed to be on that playground,
zero adults actually witnessed the particularly vicious attack. This was
not a simple schoolyard scuffle between kids. This was an escalation of the
student's continuing pattern of bullying and abuse of younger children and
it's clear their supervision failed. This is why we’ve pulled Liam from the
program.

This was a near-miss of a catastrophic injury that could have left us
talking about a permanently paralyzed kindergartner, rather than working
together to ensure it doesn't happen again.

The medical reality here could have been much worse. It's easy to dismiss
a parent as being sensationalist, but Liam’s pediatrician was very clear
that this type of injury can be severe enough that if the spinal
inflammation had progressed any further, he would have been transferred to
a Tier 1 Trauma Center for emergency surgery.

JCPRD has already refused to take any action to remove the older student
from the program. Because this happened on school property between Mize
students, we would expect the school and USD 232 to conduct their own
investigation, especially given that JCPRD is a tenant of the school and
district. I plan to make a public comment at the May school board meeting
with several questions relevant to the program's relationship and
oversight.

I am happy to provide any and all correspondence and information to the
district investigator so that we can develop a safety strategy based on
fact, rather than conjecture and inaccurate biased reporting.

Because of their refusal to take action, our family attorney has suggested
we consult with the school for a 504 evaluation with an embedded, and
mandatory, "direct line of sight" supervision plan along with a no contact
order. This is to ensure Liam is never again exposed to this other child or
left unprotected during the day. Between the trauma of this assault and the
history of ongoing targeting by this student, Liam’s ability to feel safe
at school is being substantially limited.

We've had similar conversations before. Despite this happening during
JCPRD, Liam doesn't know the difference. I need some assurance that Liam
won't be in a situation to be assaulted again - a plan that covers recess,
lunch, and all transitions.

Thank you,
Will Crowley

Monday at 1:00 PM works for me.

I want to be clear about my expectations for Monday: I am looking for a
commitment that the district is willing to assess and act on information
regarding student safety, regardless of the time on the clock. JCPRD
refuses to take action to hold their staff or these students accountable.
Their own negligence is being used as a defense. Therefore the district
must step in.

If your position is going to be that your authority or responsibility stops
strictly at 3:45 PM, and that the school will not take any action, then I’m
not sure we have much to discuss.

To give you some background before we sit down- this isn't just about one
bad afternoon. Liam claims that he has been dealing with a group of older
kids - what sounds like a clique - all school year. He’s come home telling
us stories about being punched, pushed, and chased alongside typical
schoolyard teasing.

Liam does *not *understand the difference between JCPRD and the school day.
It has been exceedingly hard for us to parse what happens during the day vs
aftercare, but we believe it has occurred exclusively during the aftercare
program.

Every time we’ve brought this up to the JCPRD program director, we were
told not to worry because there are consistently five staff members
supervising the outside area. We trusted that. We felt reassured, so we
continued to encourage him to find a teacher and walk away. Gerri can
validate that we've raised concerns about his exposure to this group in the
past.

Then April 2nd happened. When the JCPRD report finally came back, it
admitted that despite those five staff members being outside and "on duty,"
not one of them saw it happen. It raises concerns about what else they
failed to observe and prompts new questions about Liam's previous claims of
physical assault.

-Will

I would like to connect with you and learn more about the claim of ongoing

Good morning Alvie,

I'm glad Gerri included you on her latest response. You were included on
this draft (see below), along with others, so I will offer a chance to
review and address my concerns directly.

My request remains the same: that the school investigate a claim of
ongoing bullying that escalated into a dangerous assault on school grounds
and to work with me on a plan to ensure my son's safety going forward.

I am happy to provide you all reports, email correspondence, or other
information you need to make a determination.

-William Crowley

-----------------------------------------

Dr. Gibson and Members of the Board,

I’m writing to you today primarily as Liam’s father, but also as the CEO
of a company. I know firsthand that as an organization grows, sometimes the
culture and policies we strive for aren’t always embodied by staff on the
ground. Culture change is hard, and I understand that.

I’m reaching out because I believe there has been a significant
misalignment between USD 232’s mission to provide a "safe and supportive
environment" and the response I received following a battery on my son at
Mize Elementary on April 2nd.

My six year old son was subjected to physical battery on school grounds -
an undisputed occurrence that resulted in a high-impact strike to his back
that, according to his medical team, carried a literal risk of spinal
paralysis. We are fortunate that he avoided permanent injury, but the
gravity of the risk is undeniable. When I brought this incident to building
leadership, the response was that the school lacks authority to investigate
because it happened after 3:45 PM during a JCPRD program.

*Candidly, I’m not interested in escalation.* I’m not interested in a
lengthy legal battle, and I have no desire to spend my time publicly
questioning the district’s commitment to safety at the next board meeting,
in the local news, or by funding campaigns for leaders that not only
espouse the tenants of safety and support but also embody them. I want to
be a parent who supports this district, not one who has to audit it.

The argument that the district’s duty of care expires at 3:45 PM is not
supported by your own policies or Kansas law:

   - USD 232 Policy explicitly prohibits bullying and harassment "on
   school property." It does not provide an "after-hours" exclusion. K.S.A.
   72-6114 provides clear authority to suspend or expel students for willful
   violations of regulations on school grounds, regardless of the time of day.
   - As the owner and landlord of Mize Elementary, the district has a
   non-delegable duty to protect students from foreseeable harm on its
   premises. Established Kansas case law, specifically *Nero v. Kansas
   State University* and *Beshears v. USD 305*, confirms that while you
   can lease a space to a third party like JCPRD, you cannot "lease away" the
   legal responsibility for what happens on your land.
   - Unless the District’s Joint Use Agreement with JCPRD constitutes a
   total abdication of the District’s possessory interest - meaning your
   security, maintenance, and administration are prohibited from intervening
   in safety matters - then the District retains "Constructive Possession." If
   you control the building, you own the liability.
   - The "jurisdiction" defense fails entirely if the District had "Prior
   Notice." If the student involved has a documented history of behavioral
   issues during the instructional day, the District was on notice of a risk.
   Permitting a known threat to remain on-site in a less-supervised
   environment isn't an "outside-hours" incident; it is a failure of a known
   duty of care.
   - JCPRD aftercare is a custodial, fee-based service, not a "public
   park." Therefore, the "recreational use" immunities under the Kansas Tort
   Claims Act do not apply. This was a failure of supervision in a controlled
   environment.

I have to ask: If subpoenaed records were to show that the District had
prior knowledge of supervision failures or specific risks regarding this
tenant or the students involved, do you truly believe this "jurisdiction"
shield would hold up? Or would it simply demonstrate gross negligence?

I want to respectfully offer a chance to de-escalate. I would like to sit
down with the appropriate district leads to address this administratively.

My sole interest is Liam’s safety. I am not asking you to suspend or expel
this other child. I am asking for you to imagine the empty chair that
almost became a reality. I am asking for you to commit to an investigation
and honor your commitment to your own policies. I am asking you to support
the enforcement of those policies to ensure that no other child has to face
what Liam did.

I believe in the vision you’ve set for this district. I'm asking for your
help in making sure that vision extends to my son, regardless of what the
clock says.

I’m available to meet at your earliest convenience.

William Crowley

Thank you for reaching out as I would like to address some of your
concerns.  Safety, both physical and emotional, are our top priority in our

immediately.  The situation yesterday with Liam was handled with the other

contradictions.title: Incident report: witness list vs narrative

claimA.text: Teacher 'did not see the whole incident, but did see the end of the conflict.'

claimB.text: Form lists 'Staff' and 'Leigh White' as witnesses while description shows staff did not see the event.

contradictions.impact: JCPRD listed 'Staff' and a specific teacher as witnesses on the official report — but that same teacher admitted she only saw the tail end of what happened. If the only named witnesses didn't actually see the attack, the entire report is built on secondhand information.

contradictions.title: 'No medical treatment necessary' vs pediatric assessment

claimB.text: Pediatrician advised seven-day monitoring; DCF mandatory report; Tier 1 trauma center if spinal inflammation progressed; police case filed.

contradictions.impact: JCPRD checked a box saying 'no medical treatment was necessary.' In reality, Liam's pediatrician ordered seven days of close monitoring, filed a mandatory report with the state child-protection agency (DCF), and warned that if spinal swelling worsened he'd need a Level 1 trauma center. That's not 'no medical treatment.'

contradictions.title: Accidental fall vs intentional 'elbow drop'

claimA.text: Accidentally falling on him in the process.

claimB.text: Liam described this as an intentional 'elbow drop' (body weight on Liam).

contradictions.impact: JCPRD's report calls the attack an accidental fall. Liam described it as an intentional 'elbow drop' — a 9-year-old deliberately landing his full body weight on a 6-year-old. Whether this was an accident or deliberate changes everything about discipline, legal exposure, and whether police should be involved.

contradictions.title: USD 232 'no jurisdiction after 3:45' vs policy and statute

claimA.text: After 3:45 / JCPRD program means school lacks authority to investigate.

claimB.text: USD 232 policy prohibits bullying 'on school property' without after-hours exclusion; K.S.A. 72-6114 uses location-based language.

contradictions.impact: USD 232 told the parent their responsibility ends at 3:45 PM. But the district's own anti-bullying policy (JDDC) says it applies 'on school property' — no time limit. Kansas law (K.S.A. 72-6114) uses the same location-based language. The district's own rules contradict what they told this family.

contradictions.title: 'JCPRD operates independently' vs Lease §8(d)

claimA.text: JCPRD leases space from the district and operates its program independently, with its own staff, policies, procedures, and supervisory responsibilities.

claimB.text: Lessee will abide by… all rules, regulations, and policies adopted by the Board of Education of the School District…

contradictions.impact: Alvie Cater wrote that JCPRD 'operates independently, with its own staff, policies, procedures.' But the lease the district signed with JCPRD — Section 8(d) — says the opposite: JCPRD 'will abide by all rules, regulations, and policies adopted by the Board of Education.' The district's own contract contradicts the independence claim.

contradictions.title: Formal written 504 request vs phone-based closure

claimA.text: My prior email was a formal request for a 504 evaluation.

claimB.text: As I understood during our conversation, this is not the avenue you would like to move forward with at this time.

contradictions.impact: The parent sent a written email requesting a 504 evaluation. The school counselor later sent a follow-up email saying the parent chose not to pursue it — based on a phone call, not the written request. A formal written request was effectively closed through an undocumented phone conversation.

contradictions.title: Verbal 504 characterization vs fact sheet

claimA.text: Counselor verbally characterized 504 as only for kids with medical disabilities (not transcribed in emails).

claimB.text: Section 504 Parent Information Sheet content unknown — DOC-026 not extracted.

contradictions.impact: The school counselor verbally described 504 protections as only for kids with medical disabilities. The actual 504 fact sheet she sent may tell a different story — but the document hasn't been fully extracted yet, so we can't confirm whether the parent was given accurate information.

contradictions.title: The 'Alvie Trap': 'exclusively aftercare' vs full context

claimA.text: Liam does not understand the difference between JCPRD and the school day… we believe it has occurred exclusively during the aftercare program.

claimB.text: You indicated in your message that the behavior in question has occurred exclusively during the aftercare program, which places it within JCPRD's authority.

contradictions.impact: Alvie Cater pulled one sentence from the parent's email — 'occurred exclusively during the aftercare program' — and used it to argue the district had no jurisdiction. But the parent's full message also explained that a 6-year-old can't tell the difference between school and aftercare, and that the district should act regardless. Cater cherry-picked the sentence that helped the district dodge responsibility.

contradictions.title: 'Offered meeting / parent declined' vs stated reason

claimA.text: JCPRD indicated that they offered to meet with you in person… and understand that you declined that opportunity.

claimB.text: Declined because of their refusal to amend the report they filed; wants internal investigation based on facts.

contradictions.impact: Alvie Cater told the parent that JCPRD 'offered to meet' and the parent 'declined.' The parent did decline — but only because JCPRD refused to correct an incident report the parent had documented as inaccurate. The district framed this as the parent being uncooperative, when the parent was asking for basic accountability first.

contradictions.title: Scheduled meeting vs cancellation

claimA.text: Monday at 1:00 PM works for me.

claimB.text: I will go ahead and cancel the meeting.

contradictions.impact: Alvie Cater scheduled a meeting with the parent for Monday at 1:00 PM. Less than 48 hours later — the morning after the parent cited the lease agreement — Cater cancelled the meeting, saying 'it sounds like we are not aligned.' The district shut down its own resolution process the moment the parent invoked the contract.

contradictions.title: Schwanz memo 'invaluable childcare' vs 'separate entity' rhetoric

claimA.text: The programs JCPRD provides are invaluable to some of our families that need childcare during the summer and before and after school.

claimB.text: JCPRD is a separate entity that leases space from the district. / JCPRD operates independently.

contradictions.impact: Brian Schwanz, USD 232's Chief of Operations, wrote a memo to the school board calling JCPRD's programs 'invaluable to our families that need childcare.' But when the parent raised safety concerns, the district's position flipped to 'JCPRD is a separate entity.' You can't call a program invaluable family childcare when pitching it to the board, then call it an independent outside organization when something goes wrong.

contradictions.title: JCPRD Handbook 'independently in policy and procedure' vs Lease §8(d)

claimA.text: Our programs function independently in both policy and procedure. We are guests of the school.

claimB.text: Lessee will abide by… all rules, regulations, and policies adopted by the Board of Education.

contradictions.impact: JCPRD's own published handbook says 'our programs function independently in both policy and procedure. We are guests of the school.' But the lease they signed — Section 8(d) — says they must follow all school board policies. JCPRD publicly admits in writing that they don't follow the rules their contract requires. This is the strongest evidence of breach of contract.

contradictions.title: Fall 2025 assurances vs. April 2026 supervision facts (institutional credibility)

claimA.text: USD 232 (kindergarten): no intermingling of age groups at recess; kindergartners on green turf; typically 3–4 adults supervising.

claimB.text: April 2026: battery of 6-year-old by 9-year-old during JCPRD on school playground; parent documented five staff present, zero adult witnesses, mixed-age program context — independent of whether a child later used the word 'prank' under institutional pressure.

contradictions.impact: In Fall 2025, USD 232 staff wrote that kindergarten recess policy prevents mixing age groups and provides 3-4 adult supervisors. Six months later, a 9-year-old attacked Liam on the same school playground during a JCPRD program with five staff and zero witnesses. The written safety assurances the school gave the family did not match what actually happened.

claims.strength: MODERATE (if immunity did not exist); WEAK to MODERATE with KTCA
claims.keyRisk: Immunity shield on playground; Johnson County defense-favorable
claims.plainSummary: The school district owns the building where Liam was attacked. When you let someone use your property, you have a legal duty to make sure they're not hurting people — especially when you already knew about problems and did nothing. The challenge: Kansas has a law that protects government agencies from lawsuits when injuries happen on playgrounds, unless the negligence was extreme.

claims.strength: STRONG on story/KDHE; MODERATE to WEAK on tort judgment given immunity
claims.plainSummary: JCPRD had five staff members outside and none of them saw a 9-year-old attack a 6-year-old. Kansas childcare regulations require staff to know where every child is and what they're doing at all times. Five adults were present. Zero witnessed the assault. That's a supervision failure.

claims.theory: Contractual power to compel compliance + tort duty
claims.keyRisk: Students not parties to lease; speculative causation
claims.plainSummary: USD 232 has the power through the lease to force JCPRD to follow school rules. They chose not to use that power. When a landlord knows their tenant is creating dangerous conditions and does nothing, the landlord shares responsibility.

claims.title: KDHE licensing violations — JCPRD
claims.strength: STRONG as regulatory strategy; supporting for civil case
claims.keyRisk: No private cause of action; feeds other tracks
claims.plainSummary: Kansas has childcare licensing rules (KDHE) that require active supervision and timely incident reporting. Filing a complaint with the state licensing agency creates pressure even though it doesn't directly lead to a lawsuit — it creates an official government record of the failure.

claims.title: Negligent misrepresentation — incident report (JCPRD)
claims.standard: Knowledge or negligence as to falsity
claims.plainSummary: JCPRD's incident report contains statements that are contradicted by medical evidence and the teacher's own admissions. If the official report is misleading, any investigation or decision based on that report is built on bad information.

claims.title: Negligent hiring/training/retention — JCPRD
claims.keyRisk: Paper compliance vs practice; immunity again
claims.plainSummary: If JCPRD's staff weren't properly trained to supervise mixed-age groups on a playground, that's an organizational failure at the hiring and training level. This claim requires getting JCPRD's training records through discovery.

claims.title: Breach of contract — Lease Section 8(d)
claims.theory: JCPRD breached lease requirement to follow all Board policies; BYPASSES KTCA ENTIRELY
claims.strength: MODERATE to STRONG on breach; MODERATE on standing; UNCERTAIN on damages type
claims.keyRisk: Third-party beneficiary standing; personal injury damages through contract uncertain
claims.smokingGun: JCPRD Handbook Policy 1: 'programs function independently in both policy and procedure' — published institutional admission of non-compliance with §8(d)
claims.plainSummary: This is the strongest legal argument. The lease between USD 232 and JCPRD — Section 8(d) — requires JCPRD to follow every school board policy, including the anti-bullying policy. JCPRD's own handbook admits they operate 'independently in both policy and procedure.' That's a written confession of contract violation. And contract claims bypass the immunity protections that would normally shield government agencies from lawsuits.

policies.title: Bullying Prevention
policies.text: The Board of Education prohibits bullying in any form, including electronic means (cyberbullying), on or while using school property, in a school vehicle, or at a school-sponsored activity or event.
policies.relevance: No time-of-day exclusion. Covers 'on school property' — which is where JCPRD OST operates. This is one of the board policies §8(d) requires JCPRD to follow.
policies.violationDetail: JCPRD Handbook Policy 1 states programs function 'independently in both policy and procedure.' No evidence of board-policy-compliant bullying investigation after 4/2 incident.

policies.title: Bullying Prevention Plan (per K.S.A. 72-6147)
policies.text: Plan includes: clear definition of bullying, staff training, student education, formal/informal reporting procedures including anonymous reports, investigation process ('legal and ethical duty to investigate'), consistent consequences, chronic offender interventions, law enforcement referral.
policies.relevance: The plan establishes a duty to investigate. Under §8(d), JCPRD must comply. No evidence JCPRD followed this investigation process.
policies.violationDetail: JCPRD's response (DOC-009) was to say it was 'handled' without a documented investigation process matching the plan's requirements.

policies.title: Suspension & Expulsion Procedures
policies.text: Grounds include conduct which endangers the safety of others or substantially impinges upon or invades the rights of others 'at school, on school property, or at a school supervised activity' — per K.S.A. 72-6114.
policies.relevance: Location-based language without time-of-day limitation. Physical battery on school property falls within scope regardless of which program is running.
policies.violationDetail: Discipline policy exists but USD 232 declined jurisdiction over after-hours incident, citing JCPRD independence.

policies.title: Community Use of School Facilities
policies.text: The Board of Education, through the Superintendent or their designee, reserves the right to approve or reject any request for use of district facilities. School activities have first priority. Community organizations may use facilities at reasonable times and rates.
policies.relevance: Board controls facility use. JCPRD contract goes through Board consent agenda (per Schwanz memo). Board retains approval/rejection authority — cannot claim no responsibility for programs it approves.
policies.violationDetail: Policy itself not violated, but it establishes Board's control over and awareness of JCPRD's presence — contradicts 'separate entity' distancing.

policies.title: Emergency Safety Interventions
policies.text: Same-day parent notification required. Written documentation to parents no later than next school day including: events leading up, student behaviors, steps to transition, date/time/type of intervention, duration, personnel involved, space for parent feedback, invitation to schedule meeting.
policies.relevance: Sets the standard for incident documentation and parent notification. JCPRD's incident report process should align under §8(d).
policies.violationDetail: JCPRD incident report (DOC-020) was same-day but lacked the detail and parent-feedback provisions of GAAF. Report disputed by parent as inaccurate (DOC-016).

policies.title: Complaints
policies.text: Formal complaint process with complaint form available.
policies.relevance: Parent filed formal grievance (DOC-006). District response was to redirect to JCPRD and ultimately cancel meeting (DOC-014).
policies.violationDetail: Complaint was received but administrative path was closed by Alvie Cater within 48 hours.

policies.title: Safety and Security Program
policies.text: Comprehensive safety program covering Communication, Secure Facilities, and Response to Crisis. Includes lockdown systems, controlled entry, security cameras, and integrated communications for staff and first responders.
policies.relevance: District invests significantly in physical security on school property but claims no responsibility for student safety during after-school programs on that same property.
policies.violationDetail: Safety infrastructure exists but does not extend to oversight of third-party programs on school grounds.

sources.relevance: Sets the required staff-to-child ratios for Kansas childcare facilities. Relevant for analyzing whether JCPRD had enough staff for the number of children on the playground.

sources.holding: Critical incidents: immediate parent notice; written KDHE report by next working day
sources.relevance: Requires childcare facilities to notify parents immediately after a critical incident and file a written report with KDHE by the next business day. JCPRD's manager said they reported to KDHE only after the parent mentioned seeking medical care — raising questions about whether they would have reported at all.

sources.holding: Possessor of land duty to invitees regarding third-party conduct
sources.relevance: Legal framework for when a property owner has a duty to protect visitors from harm caused by other people on the property. Referenced in the key Kansas case (Nero) about government landlord responsibility.

sources.citation: Nero v. Kansas State University, 253 Kan. 567, 861 P.2d 768 (1993)
sources.holding: Governmental landowner owes reasonable care; foreseeable third-party harm; foreseeability often a fact question
sources.relevance: The key Kansas Supreme Court case establishing that a government property owner (like USD 232) owes reasonable care to people on its property when harm from third parties is foreseeable. The parent documented prior concerns — making the April 2026 attack foreseeable.
sources.keyQuote: 'a governmental landowner owes a duty of reasonable care; foreseeability of third-party harm is often a question of fact'

sources.holding: School duty limits — distinguishable: off-premises, voluntary fight context
sources.relevance: A case the defense will cite — but it's distinguishable. That case involved an off-campus, voluntary fight between older students. This case involves a 6-year-old attacked on school property during a supervised program with documented prior notice.

sources.citation: Sly v. Board of Education, 213 Kan. 415, 516 P.2d 895 (1973)
sources.holding: Prior notice of risk relevant to foreseeability
sources.relevance: Kansas Supreme Court case establishing that if a school had prior notice of a risk and didn't act, that supports a finding of foreseeability. The parent sent multiple emails warning about safety problems before the April 2026 attack.

sources.holding: School liability limits
sources.relevance: Defense case on limits of school liability. Distinguishable but will be cited by opposing counsel.

sources.citation: Honeycutt v. City of Wichita, 251 Kan. 451, 836 P.2d 1128 (1992)
sources.holding: Duty limitations
sources.relevance: Cited through the Beshears case for general duty limitations. Defense will reference it.

sources.citation: Gould v. Taco Bell, 239 Kan. 564, 722 P.2d 511 (1986)
sources.holding: Premises liability framework
sources.relevance: Premises liability framework case quoted in the Nero decision. Establishes the property-owner duty analysis.

sources.citation: Kincaid v. Dess, No. 107,970 (Kan. Ct. App. 2013)
sources.holding: Third-party beneficiary: must be intended not incidental; contract interpretation; need not be personally named; burden on claimant
sources.relevance: This Kansas case defines who can sue under a contract they didn't personally sign. The key question: were students the 'intended' beneficiaries of Lease Section 8(d), which requires JCPRD to follow school safety policies? If yes, the parent can bring a breach-of-contract claim on Liam's behalf.
sources.keyQuote: 'must be intended, not incidental; need not be personally named; burden on claimant'

sources.citation: Hartford Fire Ins. Co. v. Western Fire Ins. Co., 226 Kan. 197 (1979)
sources.holding: Unnamed class as intended third-party beneficiary
sources.relevance: Establishes that an unnamed class of people (like 'students') can be intended third-party beneficiaries of a contract. Supports the argument that students are the intended beneficiaries of the lease's safety requirements.

sources.holding: School gym recreational immunity; supervised activity doesn't defeat immunity; adopted Ozuk 'more than incidental' test
sources.relevance: Core Kansas immunity case about school gym activities. But it also adopted the 'more than incidental' test from Illinois — which is actually the foundation for arguing that JCPRD's program is educational, not purely recreational, and therefore immunity shouldn't apply.

sources.citation: Nichols v. USD No. 400, 246 Kan. 93, 785 P.2d 986 (1990)
sources.holding: Football practice — supervised/unsupervised distinction rejected for immunity
sources.relevance: Kansas case holding that just because an activity is supervised doesn't mean recreational immunity goes away. Supervision alone isn't enough to defeat the immunity defense.

sources.citation: Wright v. USD No. 379, 28 Kan. App. 2d 177, 14 P.3d 437 (2000)
sources.holding: Wrestling room as open area; follows Jackson
sources.relevance: Extends recreational immunity to indoor school spaces like wrestling rooms. Follows the Jackson decision.

sources.holding: Coach-supervised football — recreational immunity applies; constitutional challenge failed
sources.relevance: Even coach-supervised football falls under recreational immunity. Shows how broadly Kansas courts apply the immunity shield.

sources.citation: Lane v. Atchison Heritage Conference Center, 283 Kan. 439, 153 P.3d 541 (2007)
sources.holding: Primary purpose of facility not dispositive; Supreme Court reversed Court of Appeals
sources.relevance: Important Kansas Supreme Court case: the 'primary purpose' of a facility isn't what matters for immunity — you have to look at whether recreation was 'more than incidental' to the actual use. This cuts both ways depending on how JCPRD's program is characterized.

sources.citation: Zaragoza v. Board of Johnson County Comm'rs, 64 Kan. App. 2d 358, 551 P.3d 175 (2024)
sources.holding: Johnson County — broad reading of open/integral areas for recreational immunity
sources.relevance: Recent 2024 Johnson County case reading recreational immunity broadly. This is the most defense-favorable recent precedent in the exact same county where this case would be tried.

sources.citation: Patterson v. Cowley County, 53 Kan. App. 2d 442, 388 P.3d 923 (2017)
sources.holding: Immunity fails if injury tied to non-integral infrastructure
sources.relevance: A plaintiff-friendly exception: immunity doesn't apply if the injury happened in a part of the property that wasn't integral to recreational use. If the specific playground area serves the educational aftercare program, this could help.

sources.citation: Willard v. City of Kansas City, 235 Kan. 655 (1984)
sources.holding: Gross/wanton negligence standard
sources.relevance: Defines what 'gross and wanton negligence' means in Kansas — the threshold needed to overcome recreational immunity. Five staff present with zero witnesses could meet this bar.

sources.citation: Lee v. City of Fort Scott, 238 Kan. 421 (1985)
sources.holding: Gross/wanton — summary judgment where proof missing
sources.relevance: Defense will cite this for summary judgment on the gross/wanton negligence standard.

sources.citation: Bonewell v. City of Derby, 236 Kan. 589 (1985)
sources.holding: Public park context — gross/wanton emphasized
sources.relevance: Addresses gross/wanton negligence specifically in a public park context — directly relevant to a playground injury case.

sources.holding: Gross/wanton in public park context
sources.relevance: Another gross/wanton negligence standard case in the public park context.

sources.citation: Gruhin v. City of Overland Park, 17 Kan. App. 2d 388 (1992)
sources.holding: Gross/wanton can be fact issue precluding summary judgment
sources.relevance: Favorable case: Kansas court held that gross/wanton negligence can be a factual question that prevents the case from being thrown out on summary judgment. Supports keeping the case alive past early motions.

sources.citation: Plains Transport of Kansas v. King, 224 Kan. 17 (1978)
sources.holding: Regulatory violation alone insufficient without causation
sources.relevance: Caution: just because JCPRD violated a regulation doesn't automatically mean they're legally negligent. You still have to prove the violation caused the harm. The regulatory claim supports the story but doesn't win the lawsuit by itself.

sources.citation: KPERS v. Reimer & Koger Assocs., 262 Kan. 635, 941 P.2d 1321 (1997)
sources.holding: Government contractual obligations — same responsibilities as private entity in business transactions
sources.relevance: Critical Kansas Supreme Court case: when a government entity enters a contract, it has the same obligations as any private business. This means the breach-of-contract claim against JCPRD for violating Lease Section 8(d) is NOT subject to government immunity protections.
sources.keyQuote: 'government contractual obligations — same responsibilities as private entity in business transactions'

sources.citation: State ex rel. Stovall v. Reliance Ins. Co., 278 Kan. 777 (2005)
sources.holding: Intended vs incidental third-party beneficiary
sources.relevance: Framework case for determining intended vs. incidental third-party beneficiary status, cited through the Kincaid decision.

sources.holding: Burden on TPB claimant
sources.relevance: Places the burden on the person claiming third-party beneficiary status. The family will need to prove students were intended beneficiaries of Lease Section 8(d).

sources.citation: Hartford Fire Ins. Co. v. Western Fire Ins. Co., 226 Kan. 197 (1979)
sources.holding: Unnamed class as intended TPB
sources.relevance: Same as AUTH-20. Supports unnamed classes (like students) as intended beneficiaries.

sources.holding: Commons integral to gym = immune; distinguished 'pure school lunch room'
sources.relevance: Kansas case analyzing whether specific parts of a school building (like a commons area next to a gym) are 'integral' to recreational use for immunity purposes. Relevant to how the playground is characterized.

sources.citation: Abrams v. Oak Lawn-Hometown Middle School, 2014 IL App (1st) 132987
sources.holding: Cafetorium with educational uses NOT intended for recreation even during after-school event
sources.relevance: Strongest persuasive authority for the educational-purpose argument. Illinois court held that a school cafeteria used for an after-school event was NOT recreational — even during non-school hours — because the space's primary purpose was educational. This directly supports arguing that JCPRD's after-school program is educational, not recreational.
sources.keyQuote: 'Cafetorium with educational uses NOT intended for recreation even during after-school event'

sources.citation: Ozuk v. River Grove Board of Education, 281 Ill. App. 3d 239 (1996)
sources.holding: Instruction vs amusement distinction; 'more than incidental' recreational use test; adopted by Kansas in Jackson
sources.relevance: The foundational case that created the 'instruction vs. amusement' test and the 'more than incidental' recreational use standard. Kansas adopted this test in Jackson. It's the basis for arguing JCPRD's program has an educational purpose that goes beyond pure recreation.

sources.holding: Policy 1: 'programs function independently in both policy and procedure'; educational mission/vision throughout
sources.relevance: JCPRD's own published handbook for its Olathe programs. Policy 1 states: 'programs function independently in both policy and procedure.' This is an institutional admission — in writing, published publicly — that JCPRD does not follow the school board policies the lease requires. It also describes the program's educational mission throughout, which undermines the 'purely recreational' characterization.
sources.keyQuote: 'Our programs function independently in both policy and procedure. We are guests of the school.'

sources.holding: UCC consequential damages includes personal injury from breach of warranty
sources.relevance: Kansas UCC statute allowing personal injury damages for breach of warranty. It applies to goods sales, not services — so using it for a lease/services contract is legally uncertain. Needs counsel evaluation.

sources.holding: JCPRD provides 'invaluable' before/after school care; Board approves contract on consent agenda
sources.relevance: Brian Schwanz's memo to the USD 232 Board of Education requesting approval of the JCPRD rental contract. He describes JCPRD as providing 'invaluable' childcare. This destroys the 'separate entity' defense: the district's own Chief of Operations presented JCPRD's program to the board as integrated family childcare, not an independent outside organization.
sources.keyQuote: 'The programs JCPRD provides are invaluable to some of our families that need childcare during the summer and before and after school.'

sources.holding: Unlawful to conduct or maintain a child care facility for children under 16 without a KDHE license or temporary permit
sources.relevance: This is the enabling statute that makes JCPRD's KDHE license legally mandatory — not voluntary. JCPRD prominently advertises being 'fully licensed,' which means they are bound by every obligation that comes with licensure under K.S.A. 65-508. A parent enrolling a child in a licensed program has a right to expect statutory compliance.
sources.keyQuote: It shall be unlawful for any person, firm, corporation or association to conduct or maintain a maternity center or child care facility... without having a license or temporary permit therefor from the secretary.

sources.holding: Licensed child care facilities must operate 'with strict regard to the health, comfort, safety, and social welfare of children'
sources.relevance: This is the statutory duty of care for JCPRD's licensed program. It is not aspirational — it is a legal obligation attached to the KDHE license JCPRD holds. When five staff are outside and none witness an assault on a six-year-old, that is a failure of the 'strict regard to health, comfort, safety' standard. When the incident report contradicts medical evidence, that is a failure of the 'social welfare' standard.
sources.keyQuote: Each facility... shall be operated with strict regard to the health, comfort, safety, and social welfare of such children or youth.

sources.holding: Authorizes school districts to lease land, buildings, and facilities; governs the legal framework for the USD 232-JCPRD lease
sources.relevance: This is the statutory authority under which USD 232 leases space to JCPRD at Mize Elementary. The district chose to enter this lease, chose its terms (including Section 8(d)), and retains the authority to enforce them. The district cannot claim it has 'no oversight' when the lease it voluntarily created includes enforcement mechanisms.

sources.holding: Markets OST as STEM-enrichment, 'safe, enriching, fun place,' 1:15 ratio, bachelor's-degreed directors, fully KDHE licensed; 'enhanced safety, convenience' and 'extend school day learning'
sources.relevance: This is how JCPRD presents itself to parents making enrollment decisions. They promise STEM education, environmental literacy, safety, and qualified staff. They explicitly state: 'a safe, enriching, fun place to be' and that the program provides 'enhanced safety, convenience, and numerous opportunities to extend school day learning experiences.' Parents rely on these representations when entrusting their children to the program.
sources.keyQuote: The availability of this program within your child's school provides enhanced safety, convenience, and numerous opportunities to extend school day learning experiences.

sources.holding: Registration organized by school name (e.g., 'OST: Olathe - School Name'), KDHE-required ePACT forms, school-aligned enrollment windows
sources.relevance: The registration process reinforces that this is a school-integrated program, not an independent recreation offering. Parents search by their child's school name. Enrollment windows are aligned to school districts. KDHE forms are required before attendance. A reasonable parent would conclude this program operates under the same safety framework as the school itself.
sources.keyQuote: Search for your child's school name in the search bar. Click on 'OST: Olathe - School Name (2026-27)'.

sources.holding: Self-promotional badge on OST page claiming 'Voted Best After School Care'
sources.relevance: JCPRD uses this award prominently on their marketing page to build parental trust. The claim positions them as the standard of excellence for after-school care in Johnson County. When the program fails to meet basic supervision standards — five staff outside, zero witnesses to an assault — the gap between marketing and reality becomes evidence of negligent misrepresentation.
sources.keyQuote: Voted Best After School Care!

sources.holding: Defines 'extraordinary school program' as a before/after-school enrichment program established by the board of education. Kansas law treats this type of programming as educational in character — not recreational.
sources.relevance: JCPRD's marketing matches this statute's definition almost word-for-word: STEM, enrichment, 'extending school day learning.' However, JCPRD's OST does not formally qualify as an extraordinary school program because it was not 'established by the board' and is not staffed by certified teachers. The statute's value is definitional: Kansas law itself categorizes before/after-school enrichment as educational, undermining the defense's 'recreational program' characterization for immunity purposes. Use for the Ozuk/Jackson educational-purpose argument only — not as a direct classification of JCPRD's program.
sources.keyQuote: An 'extraordinary school program' means a program which is established by the board of education of a school district, operated before or after regular school hours during the regular school term, and maintained for any or all of the following purposes: (1) Providing pupils with additional time to achieve learner exit or improvement plan outcomes; (2) giving pupils remedial instruction or independent study assistance; (3) affording pupils an opportunity to strengthen or attain mastery of basic or higher order thinking skills; and (4) conducting special projects and activities designed to enrich and enhance the educational experience of pupils.

sources.holding: Authorizes school boards to establish, operate, and maintain child care facilities — including by contracting with public or private agencies — and subjects all such facilities to KDHE licensing (article 5 of chapter 65)
sources.relevance: USD 232 contracted with JCPRD for child care under the authority granted by this statute. Subsection (c) is critical: 'Every school district which establishes, operates and maintains a child care facility shall be subject to the provisions contained in article 5 of chapter 65' — that's the KDHE licensing chapter (K.S.A. 65-501 through 65-508). The district didn't just casually lease space. It entered into a statutory arrangement that explicitly binds both parties to KDHE licensing obligations, including the K.S.A. 65-508 duty of care.
sources.keyQuote: The board of education of any school district may: (1) Establish, operate and maintain a child care facility; (3) contract with private, nonprofit corporations or associations or with any public or private agency or institution... for the establishment, operation and maintenance of a child care facility. (c) Every school district which establishes, operates and maintains a child care facility shall be subject to the provisions contained in article 5 of chapter 65.

sources.holding: Defines 'school-age program' as a child care facility serving exclusively school-age children; establishes licensing framework for such programs operating in schools and public recreation centers
sources.relevance: This statute defines what JCPRD's OST is in KDHE licensing terms: a 'school-age program' — a child care facility operating in a 'school' (defined as 'any building used for instruction of students enrolled in kindergarten or any of the grades one through 12'). Mize Elementary is a school. JCPRD's OST operates in it. This statute confirms JCPRD's program is a licensed child care facility under Kansas law, not just a casual tenant. It cannot operate without KDHE licensure and is subject to all obligations that come with it.
sources.keyQuote: 'School-age program' means a child care facility that serves exclusively school-age children and youth. 'School' means any building used for instruction of students enrolled in kindergarten or any of the grades one through 12 by a school district or an accredited nonpublic school.

sources.holding: Authorizes school boards to cooperate with public agency officers managing parks and public grounds 'to provide for the supervision and instruction necessary to carry on such public educational and recreational activities'
sources.relevance: This is the statutory authority for the USD 232-JCPRD partnership. The statute explicitly uses the phrase 'educational and recreational' — the Kansas legislature itself recognized that school-agency partnerships produce hybrid programs, not purely recreational ones. This bridges the childcare classification (72-1421) and the educational character of the program (72-3239), and prevents the defense from forcing a binary choice between 'childcare' and 'recreation.'
sources.keyQuote: Such board is also authorized to cooperate with the officers having the custody and management of public buildings and public parks and other public grounds in cities, to provide for the supervision and instruction necessary to carry on such public educational and recreational activities.

sources.holding: Exempts 'extraordinary school programs' (K.S.A. 72-3239) from KDHE child care facility licensing — but only if conducted on school premises, attended by enrolled pupils only, and staffed by certified elementary school teachers
sources.relevance: This regulation confirms that true extraordinary school programs are a separate regulatory category from licensed child care. JCPRD's program does NOT qualify for this exemption: JCPRD is not a school district, its staff are not certified teachers, and it serves children from multiple schools. JCPRD chose KDHE licensure as a child care facility. This reinforces that the correct classification is licensed child care under K.S.A. 65-527/72-1421, subject to the K.S.A. 65-508 duty of care — not an exempt educational program.
sources.keyQuote: An 'extraordinary school program,' as defined in K.S.A. 72-8238, or a similar extended school day program that is conducted on the premises of an accredited non-public school, is attended only by pupils enrolled in the school, and is staffed by certified elementary school teachers [shall not be considered a child care facility].

sources.holding: Defines "child care facility," "school-age program," and "day care facility" for purposes of Article 5. A "school-age program" is a child care facility serving exclusively school-age children. This definition anchors JCPRD's OST program within the Article 5 regulatory framework.
sources.relevance: Establishes that JCPRD's Out of School Time program is a "school-age program" and therefore a "child care facility" under Article 5. This is the definitional anchor that makes every other Article 5 provision applicable.
sources.keyQuote: "School-age program" means a child care facility that serves exclusively school-age children and youth but does not include a youth development program.

sources.holding: Authorizes KDHE to revoke a child care facility license when the facility "is maintained without due regard to the health, safety or welfare of any woman or child." Revocation requires notice and hearing under the Kansas Administrative Procedure Act.
sources.relevance: Under 72-1421(c), USD 232 is subject to this provision. The standard — "maintained without due regard" — is the same language as 65-508 but here it carries a consequence: license revocation. The district's child care arrangement is exposed to this enforcement mechanism.
sources.keyQuote: When the secretary of health and environment finds...that the maternity center or child care facility is maintained without due regard to the health, safety or welfare of any woman or child, the secretary of health and environment may issue an order revoking such license.

sources.holding: Requires KDHE to notify the Department of Education and other agencies of any license limitation, modification, suspension, or revocation. The facility must also notify parents/guardians in writing of any such action.
sources.relevance: Creates a parent-notification duty. If JCPRD's license were limited or modified due to compliance issues, parents must be informed in writing. This section also triggers Department of Education involvement — linking KDHE licensing actions back to the educational system.
sources.keyQuote: A maternity center or child care facility that has had a license limited, modified, suspended, revoked or denied by the secretary of health and environment shall notify in writing the parents or guardians of the enrollees.

sources.holding: Requires every child care facility licensee to maintain records including "the name and age of each child received and cared for," the attending physician for any sick children, and parent/guardian information.
sources.relevance: JCPRD Site Coordinator Jennifer Anderson admitted the incident report "does not include later information," meaning it was knowingly incomplete. Under 65-507, the facility is required to maintain records including the name of the physician who attended any sick or injured children. An incomplete or inaccurate incident report may violate this record-keeping requirement.
sources.keyQuote: Each child care facility licensee shall keep a record...which shall include the name and age of each child received and cared for in the facility; the name of the physician who attended any sick children in the facility, together with the names and addresses of the parents or guardians of such children.

sources.holding: KDHE must inspect every child care facility at least once every 12 months. Critically, KDHE "shall conduct an inspection of any child care facility upon receiving a complaint." The licensee must give all reasonable information and afford every reasonable facility for viewing the premises.
sources.relevance: After the April 2026 assault, neither JCPRD nor USD 232 appears to have filed a complaint with KDHE, nor informed the parent of their right to trigger a complaint-based inspection. Under 72-1421(c), the district is subject to this inspection regime. A KDHE complaint inspection could evaluate playground supervision, incident reporting, and compliance with 65-508.
sources.keyQuote: The secretary of health and environment shall conduct an inspection of any child care facility upon receiving a complaint.

sources.holding: When an authorized agent finds a child care facility "not being conducted according to law," the licensee must be notified in writing and has 5 days to make the required changes or alterations.
sources.relevance: Establishes a 5-day cure period after a finding of non-compliance. This is the enforcement pipeline: complaint (65-512) triggers inspection, inspection triggers written notice (65-513), failure to cure within 5 days triggers penalties (65-514) or license action (65-523/65-524).
sources.keyQuote: It shall thereupon be the duty of the licensee to make such changes or alterations as are contained in the written notice within five days from the receipt of such notice.

sources.holding: Any person who violates Article 5 is "guilty of a misdemeanor." Each day of non-compliance is a separate offense ($5–$50 fine per day). After 30 days of continued non-compliance, premises may be closed.
sources.relevance: Violations of Article 5 carry criminal penalties. Under 72-1421(c), the district is subject to these provisions. Sustained non-compliance — such as failure to maintain adequate supervision standards or incomplete record-keeping — could constitute ongoing daily violations.
sources.keyQuote: Any person, firm, corporation or association who violates the provisions of article 5 of chapter 65...shall be guilty of a misdemeanor...Each and every day that the person fails or refuses to comply shall be deemed a separate offense.

sources.holding: The county attorney of each county is "authorized and required" to file complaints and prosecute to final determination all Article 5 violations upon complaint from an authorized KDHE agent.
sources.relevance: Creates a mandatory prosecution mechanism. The Johnson County Attorney is required to prosecute Article 5 violations upon KDHE complaint. This is not discretionary — the statute says "authorized and required."
sources.keyQuote: The county attorney of each county in this state is hereby authorized and required, upon complaint of any authorized agent of the secretary of health and environment, to file complaint and prosecute to the final determination all actions or proceedings against any person under the provisions of this act.

sources.holding: The KDHE secretary may limit, modify, or suspend any license on five grounds, including: (a) violation of the act or regulations, (b) aiding or permitting violations, and (c) "conduct in the operation or maintenance...which is inimical to the health, safety or welfare of any...child."
sources.relevance: Three of the five grounds for license suspension are potentially implicated: (a) violation of 65-508 supervision/care standards; (b) aiding or permitting violations by failing to enforce policies; (c) conduct inimical to child welfare — five staff present but zero witnesses to an assault on a six-year-old.
sources.keyQuote: Conduct in the operation or maintenance, or both the operation and maintenance, of a maternity center or child care facility which is inimical to the health, safety or welfare of any woman or child receiving services from such maternity center or child care facility, or the public.

sources.holding: KDHE may suspend a license prior to any hearing when the action "is necessary to protect any child in the child care facility from physical or mental abuse, abandonment or any other substantial threat to health, safety or welfare."
sources.relevance: The emergency suspension standard — "physical or mental abuse...or any other substantial threat" — describes what happened. A six-year-old was physically assaulted by a nine-year-old while under supervised care. This is the statutory mechanism that exists to protect children in exactly this situation.
sources.keyQuote: The secretary may limit, modify or suspend any license or temporary permit...prior to any hearing when, in the opinion of the secretary, the action is necessary to protect any child in the child care facility from physical or mental abuse, abandonment or any other substantial threat to health, safety or welfare.

sources.holding: KDHE may assess civil fines up to $500 per violation per day for any violation that "significantly and adversely" affects health, safety, or sanitation of children. This is in addition to any other penalty under Article 5.
sources.relevance: Civil fines up to $500/day per violation, on top of criminal penalties under 65-514. For sustained non-compliance across multiple provisions — supervision failures, incomplete records, failure to follow board policies — the financial exposure compounds rapidly.
sources.keyQuote: The secretary of health and environment...may assess a civil fine...against a licensee for each violation of such provisions or rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto which affect significantly and adversely the health, safety or sanitation of children in a child care facility. Each civil fine assessed under this section shall not exceed $500. In the case of a continuing violation, every day such violation continues shall be deemed a separate violation.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy KG — Use of School Facilities by Community Groups
sources.holding: Requires a school employee to be on duty whenever non-school groups use school facilities. Board must approve all lease arrangements.
sources.relevance: Lease §8(d) binds JCPRD to this policy. No USD 232 employee was on duty during JCPRD's OST program at Mize Elementary to ensure proper use of the building and grounds.
sources.keyQuote: Whenever any school facility is used by non-school groups or individuals, a school employee shall be on duty to see that the building and equipment are properly used.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy JGFB — Supervision of Students
sources.holding: Students under school jurisdiction must be supervised by school personnel. All school-sponsored activities must be supervised by an administration-approved adult.
sources.relevance: The district presents JCPRD OST as a service it "offers." If school-sponsored, the principal must coordinate supervision with approved adults. JCPRD staff were never approved by administration under this policy.
sources.keyQuote: Students shall be supervised by school personnel when they are under the jurisdiction of the school. All school-sponsored activities shall be supervised by an adult approved by the administration.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy JDDC — Student Bullying
sources.holding: Expressly prohibits bullying on school property and at all school-sponsored activities, programs, or events. Requires administration to implement a bullying prevention plan.
sources.relevance: JDDC applies "on school property" without time-of-day limitation. The administration was required to implement a bullying plan covering the JCPRD program on school grounds. No evidence this was done for JCPRD's after-school program.
sources.keyQuote: State and Federal Law and Board policy expressly prohibit bullying in any form, including electronic means (cyberbullying) and harassment at school, on school property, and at all school-sponsored activities, programs, or events.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy JDDB — Reporting Crimes to Law Enforcement
sources.holding: Principal SHALL report conduct constituting a misdemeanor or felony on school property or at school-supervised activities that resulted in or was substantially likely to result in serious bodily injury.
sources.relevance: An assault causing physical injury occurred on school property during a program the district presents as its own. The principal had a mandatory duty to report to law enforcement under this policy. No evidence a report was filed.
sources.keyQuote: Whenever a student engages in conduct which constitutes the commission of any misdemeanor or felony, at school, on school property, or at a school supervised activity and/or has been found... to have engaged in behavior... which has resulted in or was substantially likely to have resulted in serious bodily injury to others, the principal shall report such act to the appropriate law enforcement agency.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy JH — Student Activities
sources.holding: The principal is responsible for organizing and approving all student activities. All school-sponsored activities must be supervised by an administration-approved adult. Cross-references KG.
sources.relevance: If the JCPRD OST program qualifies as a school-sponsored activity (the district's website presents it as such), the principal must organize, approve, and ensure adult supervision — none of which occurred.
sources.keyQuote: The principal shall be responsible for organizing and approving all student activities. All school-sponsored activities shall be supervised by an adult approved by the administration.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy KGD — Disruptive Acts at School or School Activities
sources.holding: Persons threatening the safety of students or school personnel will be asked to leave. School administration and staff are responsible for handling any disturbance.
sources.relevance: Establishes that school administration is responsible for handling safety threats at school activities — not just during school hours. Cross-references EBC, GAAE, JCDBB, and JDDC.
sources.keyQuote: Persons threatening the safety of students, school personnel, or other persons; to damage school property; or to interfere with school or school activities or the educational process will be asked to leave the premises.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy KFD — School Volunteers
sources.holding: School volunteers are bound by all district policies, rules, and regulations and work under school staff direction.
sources.relevance: If even unpaid volunteers are bound by district policies, it is inconsistent for the district to claim a paid lessee (JCPRD) operating on school property is not. Strengthens the §8(d) obligation argument.

sources.citation: USD 232 Board Policy EBC — Security and Safety
sources.holding: Umbrella security and safety policy cross-referencing JCAC, JCDBB, JDD, JDDB, JDDC, JGGA, and KGD. Authorizes security devices and measures to prevent intrusions or disturbances on school property.
sources.relevance: Creates a web of safety obligations on school property. The cross-references to JDDB (crime reporting), JDDC (bullying), and KGD (disruptive acts) all apply to activity on school property regardless of who is operating the program.
sources.keyQuote: Security devices may be installed at district attendance centers. Other measures may be taken to prevent intrusions or disturbances from occurring in school buildings or trespassing on school grounds.

sources.holding: USD 232's own website presents JCPRD's Out of School Time program as a district service, stating the district "partners with JCPRD to offer" before/after school programming.
sources.relevance: Undercuts the "passive landlord" defense. The district presents this as its own offering to families under "Family Resources > Family and Student Services." A parent visiting the district website would reasonably conclude this is a district-operated or district-endorsed program subject to district standards.
sources.keyQuote: USD 232 partners with Johnson County Parks & Recreation District to offer before/after school programming for elementary students.

phases.title: The Setup
phases.subtitle: Board approves lease, safety assurances given, early warning signs

daySummaries.2024-06-26: USD 232 asks its board to approve JCPRD's lease — calling the program 'invaluable childcare.'
daySummaries.2025-07-07: Board approves the lease, including Section 8(d) requiring JCPRD to follow all school policies.
daySummaries.2025-09-18: School staff confirm kindergartners are never mixed with older kids at recess. Parent flags that Liam's account contradicts this policy.
daySummaries.2025-09-19: Liam calls the incidents 'pranks.' Parent works with staff in good faith to sort it out.

phases.title: The Assault
phases.subtitle: A 9-year-old attacks a 6-year-old on school grounds — five staff present, zero witnesses

daySummaries.2026-04-02: A 9-year-old physically assaults Liam on the Mize Elementary playground during JCPRD's aftercare program. Five JCPRD staff are outside. Not a single adult witnesses the attack.

phases.title: The Response
phases.subtitle: JCPRD minimizes, parent escalates to police and DCF

daySummaries.2026-04-03: JCPRD's first response frames the documented battery as a 'feeling.' Parent fires back with facts and announces DCF and police filings.
daySummaries.2026-04-04: Parent files a formal police report. Case #2601522.
daySummaries.2026-04-05: Parent notifies school: Liam will be absent for a week on pediatrician's orders.

phases.title: The Cover-Up
phases.subtitle: JCPRD's incident report contradicts medical evidence; parent documents every discrepancy

daySummaries.2026-04-06: JCPRD sends the incident report. Parent's detailed rebuttal exposes: witnesses who didn't see anything listed as witnesses, 'no medical treatment necessary' vs. pediatric escalation, 'accidental' vs. intentional. JCPRD admits the report was written day-of and doesn't include later information.

phases.title: The Deflection
phases.subtitle: 'Separate entity' — the district disclaims responsibility for its own building

daySummaries.2026-04-07: Parent lays out the full safety case to school staff. Principal responds: JCPRD is a 'separate entity' — not our problem. Parent asks point-blank: is the district refusing to investigate?
daySummaries.2026-04-08: Parent sends formal grievance citing the lease, state law, and school policy. Alvie Cater proposes a meeting. Parent accepts and sets expectations.

phases.title: The Shutdown
phases.subtitle: District uses parent's own words against him, then cancels the meeting when he cites the lease

daySummaries.2026-04-09: Alvie Cater sends the district's official position: JCPRD 'operates independently,' cherry-picks the parent's words for a jurisdiction dodge, and claims the parent 'declined' JCPRD's meeting. Parent immediately replies with the lease quote. Separately, school counselor memorializes parent's alleged 504 withdrawal from a phone call.
daySummaries.2026-04-10: Alvie Cater cancels the meeting — the morning after the parent cited the lease. Parent closes the JCPRD administrative channel and discloses pending litigation.
